# ListCollab — Build Plan

> Generated by app-build-planner skill. This is the project-level entry point for GitHub Copilot.
> Location: `.github/build-plans/listcollab/README.md`

## What You're Building

ListCollab is a shared list app for group events. An organiser creates an event (BBQ, camping trip, Christmas lunch, games night), defines what needs to be brought or done, and shares one link. Anyone with that link identifies themselves, claims part or all of what is needed, and can add contributions nobody requested. The event page shows at a glance what is covered and what is still missing.

This is a **brownfield rebuild**, not a greenfield project. The repository currently contains a single-purpose party organiser (`PartyList`) on the `listcollab` branch: React 19 + Vite + MUI frontend, Express + MariaDB API, Docker Compose deployment. The stack stays. The domain model, API, and UI are rebuilt around a central `Event` entity. There are no user accounts — access is by unguessable event token.

## Tech Stack

| Layer | Technology |
|-------|-----------|
| Frontend | React 19 + TypeScript (strict) + Vite + MUI v6 + TanStack Query |
| Backend | Node.js 22 + TypeScript (strict) + Express 4 |
| Database | MariaDB 11 (relational), accessed via `mysql2/promise` with parameterised queries |
| Auth | No accounts. Capability tokens per event: a share token (participants) and an admin token (organiser), sent in the `X-Event-Token` header |
| Deployment | Self-hosted Docker Compose on the `atlas` homelab server |
| Monorepo | Turborepo + npm workspaces |

## Key Commands

```bash
# Install dependencies (repo root — installs all workspaces)
npm install

# Run dev server (turbo runs web + api in parallel)
npm run dev

# Run tests (unit + integration, all workspaces)
npm run test

# Run tests with coverage
npm run test:coverage

# Type check
npm run type-check

# Lint
npm run lint

# End-to-end tests (requires the dev stack running)
npm run test:e2e

# Database migrations (apply all pending)
npm run db:migrate

# Roll back the most recent migration
npm run db:rollback

# Bring up the full containerised stack
docker compose up --build
```

### For GitHub Copilot (the AI agent)

1. **Read `CONVENTIONS.md`** in this directory first and in full. These rules apply to every line of code. Non-negotiable.
2. **Check `TRACKER.md`** to see the current state of the build. Identify the active phase and next task.
3. **Read the active phase file** in `phases/`. It contains your specific tasks, constraints, and completion criteria.
4. **Read `TESTING_STANDARDS.md`** (in this directory) before writing any tests. Applies to every phase.
5. **Work through phases sequentially.** Do not start a phase until all prerequisites from the previous phase are met.
6. **Mark tasks in `TRACKER.md`** as you complete them (`✅ Complete`) or if you hit a blocker (`⛔ Blocked` with a note). Do this as you go — nothing else survives between sessions.
7. **Run the per-phase test flags** at the end of each phase before moving on. Do not skip these.
8. **Refer to `TEST_PLAN.md`** for the central test strategy and coverage targets.
9. **Re-read the tracker and active phase file at the start of every session** and after any context reset. You do not retain this plan.

### For the Human Developer

1. **Extract the build plan** so that `.github/build-plans/listcollab/` sits in your repo root.
2. **Check `.github/copilot-instructions.md`** exists and lists this project in its Active Projects table. If you already had one, merge the row rather than overwriting the file.
3. **Check `.github/instructions/listcollab.instructions.md`** has an `applyTo` glob that actually matches your source files. It ships as `**` for this single-project repo. Without it, the file is never applied.
4. **Open the repo in VS Code** and switch Copilot Chat to **agent mode**. Custom instructions apply to chat and agent mode only, not to inline completions.
5. **Verify the instruction files loaded** — type `/instructions` in the chat input, or right-click the Chat view and select **Diagnostics**. Also check the References section of a chat response.
6. **Kick off a session** with an explicit read instruction, e.g.:
   `Read #file:.github/build-plans/listcollab/README.md and begin the next incomplete task in TRACKER.md`
7. **Attach the active phase file** with `#file:` at the start of longer sessions. Copilot will not open it unprompted.
8. **Review progress** in `TRACKER.md` between sessions.

## Phases Overview

| Phase | Name | Goal |
|-------|------|------|
| 1 | Stabilise the existing repo | Known defects fixed, secrets out of the repo, Docker dev environment reliably reproducible on the current code |
| 2 | Turborepo, TypeScript and test infrastructure | Workspaces in place, strict TS end to end, shared package created, every test runner installed and running |
| 3 | Domain model and migrations | Numbered migration runner plus the event-centred schema, with the existing party migrated into a real event |
| 4 | Event-centred API | Token-scoped, validated REST API over the new schema, with `required_items` removed as a separate concept |
| 5 | Frontend restructure | `App.jsx` replaced by a routed feature-folder React app rendering the new event page |
| 6 | Collaborative UX | Share link, identify-yourself, claim/unclaim with partial quantities, guest-added contributions, organiser-only structural editing |
| 7 | Responsive polish and accessibility | Mobile-first layout, empty states, snackbars, confirmations, skeletons, keyboard and screen-reader support |
| 8 | Hardening, deployment and handoff | Production Compose stack, health checks, backups, security verification, full E2E pass, documentation |

## Key Decisions

These were settled during planning. Do not re-evaluate them mid-build. If one turns out to be wrong, raise it as a blocker in `TRACKER.md` rather than silently choosing differently.

1. **The Event is the root entity.** Participants, categories and items all belong to an event. Nothing is global.
2. **`required_items` is deleted as a concept.** One `items` table with `quantity_required` (nullable) plus `item_assignments` rows. `quantity_required: null` means an ad-hoc contribution nobody asked for. Coverage is derived: `SUM(item_assignments.quantity)` against `quantity_required`.
3. **Assignment is not completion.** `item_assignments` records who is bringing how much. An item's `status` (`open` / `covered` / `completed`) is separate and never set as a side effect of assigning someone. This was a real defect in the old model.
4. **Permission model is B+C.** Anyone with the share link can identify themselves, claim and unclaim, adjust their own claim quantity, and add new items. Structural editing — event details, deleting or renaming items and categories, deleting participants, changing `quantity_required` on someone else's item — requires the admin token. No roles table, no accounts.
5. **Two capability tokens per event.** `share_token` (short, in the shareable URL) and `admin_token` (long, held by the organiser). Both are generated with `crypto.randomBytes` and compared with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.
6. **Tokens travel in the `X-Event-Token` header, never in an API query string.** The web app reads the token from the route path and puts it in the header. This keeps tokens out of API access logs and `Referer` headers. Route paths are `/e/:shareToken` and `/e/:shareToken/manage#k=:adminToken` (fragment, so the admin token is never sent to the server as part of a page request).
7. **Tokens are stored in plaintext in the database.** Deliberate tradeoff: the database is on a private homelab network and never internet-exposed, and hashing the admin token would mean an organiser who loses their link is permanently locked out. If the app is ever exposed publicly, the upgrade path is to store `sha256(admin_token)` and surface the token once at creation. Note this in the handoff docs.
8. **Zod schemas in `packages/shared` are the single source of truth for the API contract.** Types are inferred via `z.infer`, never hand-written twice. This is what makes the old `person_id` mismatch — frontend sending a field the backend silently ignored — impossible to reproduce.
9. **One aggregate read per page.** `GET /api/events/:shareToken` returns event, participants, categories, items and assignments in a single response. REST purity is not worth seven round trips on a phone at a park.
10. **TanStack Query owns server state.** No Redux, no global store. Client-only state (dialog open, current identity) is React state plus `localStorage`.
11. **MUI stays.** The old UI's problem was information architecture and a 900-line `App.jsx`, not the component library.
12. **Existing party data is migrated, not dropped.** Migration `004` moves the current people and items into a single event so the app boots with real data. It must be idempotent and must no-op cleanly on an empty database.
13. **Mobile is the primary target, not a supported breakpoint.** The app is used on a phone, one-handed, by someone handed a link a minute ago. The base layout is the phone layout and desktop is the adaptation. Every phase from 5 onward is verified at 390×844 before it is verified at desktop width, and a phase whose mobile E2E fails is not complete regardless of how it looks on a laptop. Do not build a desktop layout and make it responsive afterwards.
14. **Deferred until real use demands them:** user accounts, OAuth, email invites, push notifications, comments, WebSockets, image uploads, recurring events, calendar sync, payments, granular permissions, inventory tracking. Do not build these.

## Security Posture

ListCollab has no accounts and no login, so **the event token is the entire authorisation model**. That makes token handling, event scoping, and enumeration resistance the security-critical surface — treat them the way you would treat auth in an app that had it.

- **Data sensitivity:** low but not nil. Stored data is participant display names, event names, dates, a location string, and free-text notes. That is personal information: a location plus a date plus a guest list tells an attacker when a house is empty. Treat event contents as private.
- **Users:** external and unauthenticated. Anyone holding a link is a user. Assume links get pasted into group chats and forwarded beyond the intended group.
- **Primary threats, in order:** (1) token enumeration or brute force against `/api/events/:token`; (2) IDOR — using a valid token for event A to read or mutate rows belonging to event B; (3) stored XSS through item names, notes and participant names rendered on a shared page; (4) privilege escalation from share token to admin capability; (5) secrets leaking through the repo, logs or error responses.
- **Non-negotiables:** every mutating route resolves the event from the token and verifies row ownership before writing. Rate limiting on all token-resolving endpoints. Strict Zod validation with length caps on every string. `helmet` with a CSP. No token, credential, or full participant list in any log line. Generic error bodies in production.
- **Compliance:** no GDPR/SOC2 obligations for personal homelab use. The data-minimisation habits are still enforced: collect a display name and nothing more. No email addresses, no phone numbers, no free-text field that invites them.
